paragraphs: A big company, PwC, asked 4,000 business leaders in 71 countries about online safety. Some of them were in Ireland.
Cyber attacks are attacks on computers. Irish companies are not as ready for them as companies in other countries.
Only 17% of Irish leaders said online safety is a full part of their risk plans. Around the world, it was 41%. Only 23% of Irish firms practise for an attack often.
Irish leaders are also careful about AI. Only 6% would let AI protect their computers alone. Around the world, it was 22%.
An expert at PwC said companies must get ready now.

Irish companies are behind companies in other countries when it comes to managing cyber risk, a new survey by PwC has found. PwC asked 4,000 business and technology leaders in 71 countries, including Ireland.

Only 17% of Irish leaders strongly agreed that cyber security was a full part of their company's risk planning. Around the world, the figure was 41%. Also, only 23% of Irish companies regularly practise what to do if there is an attack, compared with 41% globally.

Irish firms also seem worried about using AI for protection. Only 6% would let AI agents protect their systems without human help, while the global figure was 22%. New quantum computers could break today's codes in the 2030s, but only 6% of Irish firms are preparing for this, compared with 21% globally.
Leonard McAuliffe of PwC Ireland said many companies are not ready for fast-changing online dangers. He said companies that prepare well will be in a better position to grow.

Irish businesses are lagging behind their international counterparts in building cybersecurity into their wider risk management, according to new research from PwC. The firm surveyed 4,000 business and technology executives across 71 countries, including Ireland.

Just 17% of Irish respondents strongly agreed that cybersecurity was fully integrated into their organisation's risk management, compared with 41% worldwide. Similarly, only 23% said their employer regularly ran exercises to test its response to an incident, against 41% globally.

Irish executives also appear cautious about artificial intelligence. Only 6% would allow AI agents to defend their systems fully on their own, compared with 22% internationally, and just 34% named protection against AI-enabled attacks as a spending priority. The report warns that quantum computing could break current encryption as early as the 2030s, yet only 6% of Irish firms are introducing quantum-resistant measures, compared with 21% globally.
Leonard McAuliffe, a cybersecurity partner at PwC Ireland, said cyber preparation must become a core business skill, as many organisations remain unprepared for a rapidly changing threat landscape.
Irish companies are trailing their global peers when it comes to embedding cybersecurity in their broader approach to risk, a PwC survey of 4,000 executives in 71 countries suggests.

A mere 17% of Irish respondents strongly agreed that cyber risk was woven into their organisation's overall risk management, well short of the 41% recorded worldwide. Likewise, only 23% said their employer routinely rehearsed its response to a breach, again compared with 41% globally.

Irish bosses seem notably wary of handing the reins to artificial intelligence: a paltry 6% would let AI agents defend their systems autonomously, versus 22% internationally. Meanwhile, the looming threat of quantum computing, which could render existing encryption obsolete as soon as the 2030s, is being tackled by just 6% of Irish firms, compared with 21% elsewhere.

Leonard McAuliffe, a cybersecurity and privacy partner at PwC Ireland, cautioned that in the scramble to reap the rewards of AI, cyber readiness must become a core competence. Firms that get this right, he argued, will be better placed to innovate and withstand disruption.

Furthermore, although quantum computing could potentially compromise existing encryption by the 2030s, a mere 6% of Irish firms are implementing quantum-resistant safeguards, in contrast to 21% worldwide.

Leonard McAuliffe of PwC Ireland maintained that cyber preparedness must become a fundamental business capability.
